name: Salinity / elevated root-zone EC stress
summary: Salinity/high-EC stress is an exposure-response diagnosis in which measured dissolved salts coincide with impaired Cannabis growth, physiology, or yield. EC reports total ionic conductivity but not which ions caused it: direct Cannabis experiments produced different responses when EC was raised with NaCl, concentrated nutrients, hydroponic solution, or aquaponic solution. Brown tips, chlorosis, wilt, and necrosis are therefore nonspecific and require plant-linked EC trends, solution composition, pH, moisture, roots, and matched controls.
affectedParts: irrigation water, nutrient solution, substrate, or root zone
sampled leaves of documented age and canopy position
stems, leaves, inflorescences, biomass, and yield secondarily
stages: all production stages with a measured saline or concentrated-nutrient exposure
indicators: Measured irrigation or root-zone EC is elevated relative to the established crop baseline while growth declines
Growth suppression occurs together with a documented saline or high-salt root-zone exposure
Leaf nutrient imbalance appears after a measured salinity increase rather than an isolated single-element withholding pattern
Repeated plant-linked measurements show EC rising before or with reduced canopy expansion, leaf chlorophyll index, biomass accumulation, or yield relative to a matched same-cultivar control.
The affected distribution follows a documented solution, tank, irrigation zone, emitter, recirculation loop, container, or substrate-extraction pattern rather than a random lesion pattern.

Water, nutrient-solution, substrate-extract, or tissue chemistry identifies the ions or fertilizer concentration that produced the conductivity; EC alone does not identify sodium, chloride, or any single nutrient.

Visible leaf necrosis may appear under severe NaCl exposure, but one Early Haze rockwool trial observed it only at its two highest NaCl EC treatments while growth or yield effects occurred without that sign.

Direct studies show that production system and salt composition alter the response: hydroponic and aquaponic solutions differed under the same NaCl treatments, and nutrient-raised EC differed from NaCl-raised EC.
exclusions: Do not label salinity or “nutrient burn” from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting without a plant-linked EC measurement and exposure history.
If EC is stable within the established crop baseline and no saline, concentrated-fertilizer, source-water, recirculation, or accumulation pathway is documented, investigate another cause.
Measure root-zone water content across representative center, edge, and depth positions because simple drought, preferential wetting, or a failed emitter can resemble osmotic stress.
Exclude overwatering and hypoxia with irrigation history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; a wet root zone does not prove salts are causal.
Measure root-zone pH and review tissue or solution chemistry because abnormal pH or a verified single-element deficiency or toxicity can create a similar canopy pattern.
Inspect intact roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, galled, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain organism confirmation when root disease or nematodes remain plausible.
Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, airflow, and recent spray history to exclude heat, light, high atmospheric demand, droplet, and contact injury.

Check root-ball geometry, substrate compaction, container temperature, and root restriction because small or uneven root volume can produce localized water and nutrient stress without primary salinity.

progression.description: A source-water, fertilizer, recirculation, evaporation, drainage, or salt-addition event changes the measured input or root-zone EC; no reliable visible sign may yet be present.
Plant water relations, chlorophyll index, gas exchange, nutrient uptake, or canopy expansion may diverge from matched controls before a specific color or morphology appears.

The T1 nutrient-input experiment reported no visible treatment injury despite solution accumulation. Preserve this negative result separately from NaCl injury; a normal-looking canopy does not measure nutrient concentration or identify ions.
Repeated whole-plant views may show reduced height, width, leaf production, biomass, or inflorescence growth, but the pattern depends on cultivar, stage, medium, solution type, and ion mixture.

Necrosis or broader decline may develop under severe exposure; direct Early Haze evidence limits visible necrosis to extreme NaCl treatments in that study and does not validate brown tips as a general threshold.

After the documented salt source and root-zone conditions are corrected, compare EC and new growth over time; old necrotic tissue does not reverse, and absent recovery triggers pH, moisture, root, vascular, and pathogen investigation.

lookAlikes: Abnormal root-zone pH or mixed nutrient lockout
Boron, manganese, or other nutrient toxicity
Foliar spray, disinfectant, or contact injury
confirmation: Calibrate the EC and pH meters and record input water, mixed solution, and representative root-zone or leachate values with the extraction method, temperature compensation, units, date, and plant or irrigation-zone identity.
Sample multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions or multiple emitters and containers; compare the trend with the established production baseline and a matched same-cultivar unaffected control.

Document fertilizer products, mixing order and concentration, source-water analysis, sodium and chloride inputs, irrigation volume, drainage fraction, recirculation history, evaporation, and any tank or dosing fault.
When the salt source is uncertain, obtain solution, substrate-extract, and tissue analysis for sodium, chloride, and relevant macro- and micronutrients; do not infer ion composition from EC.
Measure root-zone moisture, pH, and temperature and record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at the same time as each visual capture.

Inspect and photograph the intact root ball, crown, drainage pattern, emitter placement, and root color and firmness; use diagnostic testing when disease, nematodes, or vascular injury remains plausible.

Capture fixed whole-plant front and side views plus top, upper-leaf, lower-leaf, margin, underside, root-zone, meter-display, and source-label views at the same time of day before exposure, during the EC rise, before correction, and during recovery.

Record flowering day separately from days since salt exposure and solution renewal; preserve each solution-specific concentration and panel identity. Do not compare the hydroponic 1/5 mM curves with aquaponic 4/8 mM curves as equal-dose controls or treat the study renewal schedule as a corrective prescription.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, meter-unlinked, composition-unknown, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed salinity class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Verify the reading with a calibrated meter and a medium-appropriate sampling method before changing fertilizer or irrigation.
Record moisture, pH, roots, solution composition, and the affected irrigation zone before corrective actions erase the exposure evidence.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented salt source, dosing fault, source-water problem, recirculation accumulation, or root-zone concentration with a crop- and medium-specific plan; this record does not prescribe a universal flush volume or target EC.
Trend input and root-zone EC, moisture, pH, new growth, and matched controls after correction; investigate coexisting root or environmental injury if recovery does not follow.
prevention: Trend calibrated input and root-zone EC with consistent sampling methods, units, temperature handling, crop stage, and irrigation-zone identity.
Account separately for source-water ions, fertilizer formulation, drainage, recirculation, evaporation, substrate, container size, cultivar, and crop stage when establishing baselines and alerts.
warnings: EC is a conductivity measurement, not an ion identity: the same EC can be produced by NaCl or by different nutrient mixtures with different Cannabis responses.
The published 1.8 to 12 mS/cm, 1 to 40 mM NaCl, and 0.4 to 6 dS/m treatments are study-specific exposures, not universal safe, toxic, correction, or training-label thresholds.
Do not diagnose “nutrient burn” or salinity from brown tips, marginal necrosis, chlorosis, curl, wilt, dark foliage, or stunting alone; photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.20.

Visible necrosis was restricted to the highest NaCl treatments in one Early Haze rockwool experiment, while other measured effects occurred without that sign; absence or presence of necrosis is not decisive.

The evidence spans one drug-type chemovar, Early Haze, and Felina 32 fiber hemp under distinct hydroponic, aquaponic, rockwool, mesocosm, nutrient, NaCl, and biostimulant conditions; cultivar and system transfer requires human review.

Two CC BY treatment-response diagrams are indexed as reference context, but neither is a symptom photograph, a plant-linked diagnostic sequence, or a verified diagnostic video; automated training eligibility remains false.

sources.title: Effect of saline irrigation and plant-based biostimulant application on fiber hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) growth and phytocannabinoid composition
supportedClaims: Felina 32 fiber hemp in an outdoor mesocosm was irrigated with NaCl solutions at 2, 4, and 6 dS/m and compared with a 0.4 dS/m tap-water control.
The 2, 4, and 6 dS/m irrigation treatments limited crop growth by 7%, 30%, and 48%, respectively; biomass effects followed measured salinity rather than a diagnostic leaf-color class.

The experiment documented altered sodium, chloride, phosphate, nitrate, potassium, and calcium assimilation in leaves, supporting broad mineral imbalance as a measured consequence rather than proof of a single-element deficiency.

Because the study used one fiber cultivar, NaCl-defined irrigation treatments, an outdoor mesocosm, and a biostimulant factor, its EC values are treatment conditions rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Aquaponic and Hydroponic Solutions Modulate NaCl-Induced Stress in Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: A controlled indoor flowering experiment tested one type-II chemovar at 1 to 40 mM NaCl in hydroponic and aquaponic solutions and measured canopy growth, chlorophyll content index, gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, water-use physiology, solution pH/EC, yield, and cannabinoids.
At 40 mM NaCl, hydroponic plants had reduced growth index and chlorophyll content index over time, while the same measured responses were not significantly affected by NaCl in the aquaponic solution.

Figure 1 reports weekly canopy growth-index trajectories for 1, 5, 10, 20 and 40 mM NaCl in hydroponic panel A, versus 4, 8, 10, 20 and 40 mM in aquaponic panel B. The low-dose treatments differ; this is a response diagram, not a symptom photograph or universal threshold.

Figure 2 reports chlorophyll content index from the most recently expanded center leaflet over the same flowering-stage treatments; the hydroponic 40 mM treatment declined while the aquaponic panel did not show the same NaCl response.
The solution-dependent result and single-chemovar flowering design show that production system, genotype, stage, and treatment composition must accompany any image or video label.
The study did not establish a universal visible symptom signature; image appearance alone cannot identify NaCl exposure or elevated root-zone EC as the primary cause.

Treatments began on flowering day 12 after 11 days in a common nutrient solution; the figure axes report days in flowering, not days since NaCl exposure. Preserve both clocks when annotating response timing.

All plants received fresh treatment solutions when any plant exceeded the specified pH-change, depletion or EC-change trigger, or every seven days otherwise. This renewal protocol differs from uninterrupted salt accumulation in an unmanaged reservoir.

sources.title: Salinity effects on yield and nutrient uptake in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Early Haze Cannabis was grown hydroponically in rockwool at 1.8, 3, 6, 9, or 12 mS/cm, with EC raised either by increasing N, P, K, Ca, Mg, and S together or by adding NaCl to the 1.8 mS/cm nutrient solution.
Shoot and bud weight declined under both EC-raising pathways, but the response boundaries differed, demonstrating that equal EC does not identify the salt composition or a single causal ion.

Visible leaf necrosis occurred only in the 9 and 12 mS/cm NaCl treatments; absence of necrosis did not exclude yield effects, and necrosis at those extreme study treatments is not a universal field threshold.

Low leaf phosphorus in some low-EC treatments was associated with root-zone pH above 7.5, showing why pH and tissue chemistry must be checked rather than treating EC or leaf appearance as a single-nutrient diagnosis.

The trial used one cultivar, rockwool, hydroponic nutrient solutions, and deliberately constructed EC treatments; transfer to other cultivars, media, salt mixtures, and irrigation systems requires human review.

sources.title: Elevated root-zone P and nutrient concentration do not increase yield or cannabinoids in medical cannabis
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science; Utah State University Crop Physiology Laboratory
supportedClaims: Two trials used high-CBD T1 cuttings in closed, aerated deep-flow hydroponics through 56 days of reproductive growth. Refill EC treatments were 2 or 4 mS/cm, with P inputs from 15 to 90 mg/L; these were nutrient-supply treatments, not a NaCl challenge.

Higher nutrient input increased solution accumulation without significantly improving yield or quality, and the study reported no leaf necrosis or other visible treatment effects. A measured nutrient excess therefore did not define a visible injury class in this experiment.

The reported treatment EC was the daily refill-solution EC; tub EC and pH were measured before refill. Nominal input treatment values and the evolving closed root-zone composition are distinct measurements.

Hydroponic and aquaponic panels represent different solution contexts and must not be collapsed into a single visual salinity class.
The 1–40 mM NaCl treatments, one chemovar, continuous root exposure, and flowering-stage design are study-specific and are not universal EC or action thresholds.
Keep the whole figure, axes, treatment legend, panel identities, caption, and attribution together; do not relabel a plotted point as specimen-level ground truth.
